ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness | Kansas City, MO
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Kansas City, MO: UT thickness surveys and weld inspection on vessels, piping, tanks and structural steel at your site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Kansas City, Missouri
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Kansas City, Missouri: wall thickness surveys on corroded vessels, piping and tank shells, and angle-beam examination of welds in structural steel, pressure equipment and fabricated assemblies. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, rail facility, yard or fabrication shop, work to a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a UT inspection quote for your Kansas City site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Kansas City

Kansas City is a major rail junction on the Missouri River. The area's development council calls the metro the largest rail hub in the nation, with four Class I railroads and four intermodal parks, and Port KC is building a river terminal on 415 acres of former steel mill land where the Blue River joins the Missouri. Around that freight network sits a working industrial base: food and beverage plants, biologics and animal-health manufacturing, automotive and battery supply factories, agricultural processing, and a long list of steel fabricators.

That mix creates steady demand for ultrasonic work on equipment that wears from the inside:

  • Process piping and vessels at food, beverage and chemical plants, where steam, condensate and wash-down chemistry thin carbon steel over time.
  • Boilers, deaerators, receivers and compressed-air tanks in plant utility rooms, which fall under Missouri's boiler and pressure vessel program.
  • Aboveground storage tanks at fuel, chemical and agricultural terminals along the river and rail corridors.
  • Structural groove welds in building frames, crane runways and bridge girders, where the contract calls for volumetric examination.
  • Plate and heavy sections at fabrication shops before the steel ships, to find laminations a visual check cannot see.
  • Hopper cars, tank cars and rail maintenance infrastructure, where the owner's maintenance program names ultrasonic thickness as the check.

What UT finds in Kansas City steel, and what it misses

An ultrasonic probe sends a short burst of sound into the metal and listens for echoes. A back-wall echo measures how thick the metal is; an echo that comes back early means something reflected the sound before the far surface. That makes the method the standard answer to two questions: how much wall is left, and is there a planar flaw inside this weld. It is a volumetric method, so it sees inside a section that magnetic particle and penetrant testing cannot reach.

It has real limits, and a good technician states them in the report. Rough, scaled or heavily pitted surfaces scatter the sound and weaken the signal. Very thin material can fall inside the instrument's dead zone. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic stainless welds distort the beam and can hide flaws. A planar flaw lying parallel to the sound path reflects almost nothing, which is why weld scans use several beam angles from both sides of the joint. The method also needs a couplant film between probe and metal, so a dry, cracked or flaking surface has to be prepared first.

Thickness testing: how a corrosion survey is done

Most Kansas City ultrasonic work is thickness measurement. The technician sets up a dual-element probe, which has separate transmit and receive crystals and copes better with corroded and pitted surfaces than a single-element probe, and calibrates it on a step block made of the same material as the component. Readings are taken at condition monitoring locations, usually laid out as a grid on a vessel head, an elbow or a tank shell course, and each location is marked so the next survey reads the same spot. Contact pulse-echo thickness measurement is covered by ASTM E797 and by SE-797 in Article 23 of ASME Section V.

Three details separate a defensible survey from a quick one. First, the A-scan display stays on screen, so the technician can tell a true back-wall signal from a doubled echo or a lamination reading that looks like thin wall. Second, hot lines need high-temperature probes, suitable couplant and a temperature correction, because sound travels more slowly in hot steel. Third, the lowest reading in each grid is recorded with its location rather than averaged away, because the owner's inspector sets the corrosion rate from the minimum. For code background, see the guide to ASME Section V Article 5 thickness measurement.

Weld examination with angle beams

For welds, the technician switches to angle-beam shear-wave probes, normally 45, 60 or 70 degrees, chosen for the joint geometry and plate thickness. A reference level, often a distance-amplitude curve built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, sets the sensitivity. The probe is scanned along both sides of the weld, and across it where the procedure requires, looking for lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, cracks and slag lines. Each indication is plotted for position, length and amplitude, then compared with the acceptance table.

The governing document depends on the job. ASME Section V Article 4 gives the technique for welds; ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 sets ultrasonic acceptance for pressure vessel welds; ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.6 covers process piping; and AWS D1.1 Clause 8 in the 2020 edition covers ultrasonic examination of groove welds in structural steel. These are different tables with different rules, so the job starts by confirming which one the engineer has named. Where an owner wants ultrasonic examination of production welds in place of radiography, that substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and any authorized inspector before work begins.

Codes, acceptance criteria and Missouri's boiler and pressure vessel law

Missouri regulates boilers and pressure vessels in service through the Division of Fire Safety, under RSMo 650.200 through 650.295 and 11 CSR 40-2. New units must be built to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and registered with the National Board. Most objects are inspected about every two years, the owner is responsible for the certificate inspection whatever a service contract says, and the Division inspects equipment that has no insurance carrier while insurers inspect what they cover. Ultrasonic thickness data supports those inspections; it does not replace the duties of the state or insurer inspector.

Other regimes sit alongside it. API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground storage tanks put the owner's authorized inspector in charge of the inspection, and Atlantis supplies the NDE data: thickness at condition monitoring locations, and indications with size and position. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires mechanical integrity inspection at covered process plants, following recognized good engineering practice. PHMSA rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 apply to regulated pipelines. The Kansas City metro also straddles the state line, so work on the Kansas side falls under Kansas rules, and the owner's inspector confirms which jurisdiction applies.

Who does the work, and what the report contains

Technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the examination and interprets the results; an ASNT Level III writes and approves the procedure and reviews reports. The company's Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel, which is why a customer audit looks at the written practice rather than at a card from an outside body.

A Kansas City ultrasonic report names the component and its identification, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the technician and level, the surface condition and temperature, and the date. For thickness work it includes a grid sketch with every reading, the minimum per location and the comparison with the previous survey or nominal wall. For weld work it lists each recordable indication with position, length and amplitude and states accept or reject against the named table. The complete UT guide explains the underlying method in more depth.

Planning a UT job in Kansas City

Weather and site logistics shape a Kansas City job more than most owners expect. Winter cold thickens couplant, so a cold-weather procedure uses a couplant rated for the temperature and keeps probe and block close to the part's temperature. Summer heat and humidity make long shifts on tank roofs and rack piping slow, and hot lines need the high-temperature setup described above. Spring and fall are the busy outage months for food, power and chemical plants, so booking early helps.

Expect the usual site requirements: badging and safety orientation at plants, track protection and flagging at rail facilities, scaffolds or lifts for elevated welds, and surface preparation by the owner. Atlantis has no office in Kansas City, so technicians travel to your site, and travel for the agreed scope is part of the quotation. Tell us the component list, material, nominal thickness, access and the code in the contract, and we can quote from that.

UT, MT or PT for your Kansas City job

Choose by the question you need answered. If you need to know how much wall remains, or whether a weld has internal lack of fusion, ultrasonic testing is the answer. If you are looking for a surface crack at a weld toe on carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Kansas City is faster and more sensitive at the surface. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic material, liquid penetrant testing in Kansas City finds surface-breaking flaws. Many repairs use two methods in sequence, for example a surface method on the excavation and ultrasonic testing on the finished weld.

Training your own UT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, Atlantis trains employer-based UT staff under SNT-TC-1A: see UT Level 1 training, UT Level 2 training, the UT practice simulator and the Kansas City NDT training page. Your employer remains responsible for certifying the people it trains. Companies that need a written practice or procedure review first can use our Level III consulting.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Kansas City?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Kansas City. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, yard or shop for the agreed scope, and the quotation includes the travel. The work itself is performed under the company's written practice, with a Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing measure on a pipe or vessel?
faq.a: It measures the remaining wall thickness at marked locations by timing the echo from the far surface. Repeating the survey at the same locations lets the owner's inspector calculate a corrosion rate and decide the next inspection date.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness on a hot line at a Kansas City plant?
faq.a: Often yes, with a high-temperature probe, couplant rated for the surface temperature and a correction for the slower sound velocity in hot steel. The safe temperature limit depends on the equipment, so tell us the operating temperature when you ask for a quote.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have their own ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII permits it in place of radiography under specific conditions. Agree the substitution with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector before the job.

faq.q: Can UT inspect stainless steel welds?
faq.a: It can for many thicknesses and joint types, but austenitic weld metal has a coarse grain that scatters and bends the beam, so the procedure usually needs a special reference block and the results carry more uncertainty. Penetrant testing is the usual surface check on stainless.

faq.q: What does a Kansas City plant need to prepare before a UT job?
faq.a: Provide access (scaffold, lift or ladder), a surface free of loose scale and flaking paint at the test locations, the equipment drawings and identification, and the inspection history. Confirm badging, safety orientation and any lockout steps so technicians are not held at the gate.

faq.q: What does the UT report include?
faq.a: It names the component, procedure and revision, instrument and probe, calibration block, technician and level, and conditions. Thickness reports add a grid of readings with minimums; weld reports list each recordable indication with location, length and amplitude and an accept or reject against the named code.

faq.q: Does Missouri require ultrasonic testing on boilers and pressure vessels?
faq.a: Missouri requires periodic certificate inspections of covered boilers and pressure vessels, generally about every two years, but the state inspector or insurer decides what the inspection includes. Ultrasonic thickness data is often collected in support, particularly when wall loss is suspected.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for ultrasonic inspection in Kansas City?
faq.a: Send the component list, material, nominal thickness, access conditions, code and preferred dates through the quote form. We reply within one business day, and the quotation sets out scope, procedure, reporting and travel.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Kansas City, MO | MPI
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) in Kansas City, MO for crane steel, bridge connections, weld toes and machine parts, at your site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Kansas City, Missouri
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection in Kansas City, Missouri, on carbon and low-alloy steel: weld toes and repair excavations, crane and lifting components, bridge and building connections, and machine parts that carry fatigue loads. Technicians are mobilized to your site carrying their own yokes, particles and light meters, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request an MPI quote for your Kansas City site and we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing is used in Kansas City

Kansas City steel works hard and moves a lot. Freight cars, locomotives and rail facilities run through the metro; the Missouri River and its tributaries need long steel bridges; and the area's plants and warehouses depend on cranes, hoists and conveyors. Fabrication shops cut, weld and ship structural steel across the Midwest, and automotive and agricultural equipment makers work with heavy welded frames. Each of these is a fatigue environment, and fatigue cracks start at the surface, which is exactly where a magnetic method looks.

Typical MT work in this market includes:

  • Weld toes and attachment welds on crane runway girders, monorails and hoist structures at plants and warehouses.
  • Lugs, hooks, shackles, spreader beams and other rigging hardware before a lift campaign.
  • Connections on steel highway and rail bridges, where cracks form at floor beam and bracing details.
  • Repair excavations in carbon steel pressure equipment, checked after grinding and again after welding.
  • Press frames, shafts, gears and other ferromagnetic machine parts during rebuilds at manufacturing plants.
  • Grain and material-handling structures, such as leg supports and conveyor frames at agricultural processing sites.

A Kansas City example: hunting fatigue cracks in a two-girder river bridge

A published engineering study of the I-435 Missouri River bridge shows why this method matters on bridges. The steel superstructure has parallel two-girder spans, so there is little redundancy if one girder cracks. Engineers carried out a hands-on fracture-critical examination that included magnetic particle testing, lightly grinding paint and weld overlap where access was blocked, and found cracking at more than 75 locations. They attributed it to out-of-plane displacement and restraint at the connections between floor beams, lateral members and the main girders. The lesson is general: bridge cracks sit at details, not in the middle of plate, and an examiner needs to be close enough to touch the steel.

That study was performed by other parties for the bridge owner and is cited here only as public context. Atlantis does not claim to have worked on it. What it shows is the type of detail that a magnetic particle technician is asked to examine on any similar structure.

What magnetic particle inspection finds, and what it misses

When a ferromagnetic part is magnetized, a crack or seam at or just under the surface interrupts the field and forces some of the flux out into the air. Fine iron particles applied to the surface gather at that leakage and outline the flaw as a visible line. The method therefore works on carbon steel and most low-alloy steels, and it does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or titanium, which are not ferromagnetic.

Sensitivity falls quickly with depth, so a flaw buried below the surface is not shown, and the method says nothing about wall thickness or internal lack of fusion; ultrasonic testing covers that ground. Orientation matters as well. A crack running parallel to the field produces almost no leakage, so the surface is magnetized in two directions at roughly right angles. Geometry can also mislead: sharp changes of section, hardness boundaries and magnetic writing from earlier handling create non-relevant indications that the technician must recognize and keep off the reject list.

Surface condition and coatings on Kansas City steel

Surface preparation decides how good a magnetic particle result is. Steel that has stood outdoors on a rail siding or a river terminal carries mill scale, rust and layers of paint, and all three keep particles from sitting where the flux leaks. The procedure sets how much coating can stay: a thin, tightly bonded film may be acceptable if the technique was demonstrated at that thickness, while thick or flaking paint must come off at the test locations. Weld spatter and sharp ridges are ground flush, because they trap particles and produce false indications.

On bridge and crane work the owner often prefers to grind only a narrow band along each weld and repair the coating afterward. That is a reasonable compromise, as long as the band covers the weld and the heat-affected zone on both sides, since toe cracks begin in that zone. Technicians record the prepared width and the coating state in the report so a later examiner knows what was and was not seen.

Technique: yokes, prods, particles and light

Most field work in Kansas City uses an electromagnetic yoke, which is portable, needs no burn marks on the part and lets the technician reposition the poles to change field direction. ASME Section V Article 7 requires an alternating-current yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke to lift at least 40 pounds. Prods and coils are used on thick sections or long parts, where a yoke cannot drive enough flux.

Particles come two ways. Dry powder, usually in a contrasting color, suits rough weld surfaces and elevated temperatures. Wet suspensions of fluorescent particles give the highest sensitivity: they are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, with the intensity and ambient light limits in the code. On dark or rough steel, a thin white contrast paint can improve visibility of colored particles. After the examination, parts that will be welded, machined or put into service near sensitive equipment may need demagnetizing so residual fields do not deflect arcs or attract chips; the procedure states when.

Codes, acceptance criteria and the Missouri regime

The method is written down in ASME Section V Article 7, in ASTM E709 as a guide and in ASTM E1444 as a practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for state highway bridges. See the Article 7 requirements explained for a plain-language walkthrough.

Missouri's Division of Fire Safety administers the state boiler and pressure vessel law, and certificate inspections of covered equipment are the owner's responsibility. Where in-service rules such as API 510, API 570 or API 653 apply, the owner's authorized inspector directs the inspection, and Atlantis reports the crack indications found. Steel highway bridge work is normally governed by the owner's specifications and AWS D1.5, and the bridge owner decides what happens to any crack found.

Who performs the inspection, and what the report shows

A Level II technician qualified under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, performs and interprets the examination. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report; that is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A each employer certifies its own people, so ask any contractor for its written practice before awarding work.

The report identifies the component, the procedure and revision, the yoke or other equipment with its calibration date, particle type and color, light meter readings for fluorescent work, the technician and level, and the surface condition. It records each indication with its location, length and orientation, with a sketch or photograph, and states accept or reject against the named criteria. Demagnetization, if required, is recorded as well.

Fatigue, repairs and weld toes: reading indications

Not every indication is a defect, and interpretation is where experience pays. A fatigue crack at a weld toe usually appears as a sharp, continuous line that follows the toe and may be slightly curved. A lap or seam shows as a tight, straight line running with the rolling direction. Magnetic writing from a chain, a magnet or an earlier examination looks like a fuzzy band that disappears after demagnetizing. A sharp change of section, such as a fillet radius, can collect particles without any crack beneath it.

The technician therefore re-examines doubtful indications, lightly dresses the area if the procedure allows and checks again, and measures the length of each recorded indication. Reject limits in the construction code are written in terms of linear indication length and spacing. Where a crack is confirmed, the owner's engineer decides on repair, and a repair is normally followed by a second examination to show the excavation is clean before welding, and again after the final pass.

Planning an MPI job in Kansas City

Kansas City weather swings from hard winter freezes to hot, humid summers. In cold conditions the carrier fluid in wet suspensions and the surface of the part both matter, and a wind-exposed bridge or tank deck needs shelter for fluorescent work because ambient white light washes out the indications. In summer, hot steel in the sun dries wet particles too fast and shortens the time to read an indication, so shading is often required. Plant outages in spring and fall tend to fill schedules, so ask early.

Atlantis has no office in Kansas City, so technicians travel to your site. Bridge and rail work adds traffic control, track protection, fall protection and access by lift or rope-free platforms arranged by the owner. Paint, rust and weld spatter at the test locations must be removed to the extent the procedure demands. Send us the component list, material, access and code through the quote form and we will plan from there.

MT, PT or UT for your Kansas City job

Pick the method by material and question. On carbon steel where you suspect surface cracking, magnetic particle testing is usually the fastest answer; the MT versus PT comparison explains the trade-offs. On stainless steel, aluminum or other non-magnetic metal, use liquid penetrant inspection in Kansas City. When the concern is internal, such as wall loss or incomplete fusion, choose ultrasonic testing in Kansas City. The national service pages for magnetic particle testing describe the full scope.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers who prefer to qualify their own staff can enrol technicians in MT Level 1 training or MT Level 2 training, read the complete magnetic particle guide and check eligibility with the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker. See the Kansas City training page for how the course and employer-led practical fit together.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Kansas City for magnetic particle work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Kansas City. Technicians are mobilized to your site with their own yokes, particles and light meters for the agreed scope, and the quotation covers travel and the written procedure.

faq.q: Which materials can magnetic particle inspection test?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials: carbon steel, most low-alloy steels and some martensitic stainless grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and titanium cannot be magnetized, so penetrant testing is used on those materials instead.

faq.q: Why does the technician magnetize in two directions?
faq.a: Flux leakage is strongest when a crack crosses the magnetic field and nearly absent when the crack runs along it. Examining twice, with the field at roughly right angles, makes cracks in any direction visible. The code requires it for that reason.

faq.q: Can MPI be done through paint or coating?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings can sometimes be tolerated if the procedure was demonstrated at that coating thickness, but loose paint, scale and weld spatter must come off. Heavier coatings weaken the leakage field and hide fine indications, so surface preparation is agreed before the job.

faq.q: When does a part need demagnetizing after MPI?
faq.a: When a residual field would affect later operations, such as welding, machining, bearing surfaces or nearby instruments. The procedure states whether demagnetization is required and how residual field is checked, and the report records that it was done.

faq.q: What is the difference between wet fluorescent and dry powder MPI?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area and are the most sensitive. Dry powder is simpler and tolerates rough welds and higher surface temperatures, but is less sensitive. The code and the application decide which is appropriate.

faq.q: Can you inspect a steel bridge in the Kansas City area?
faq.a: Atlantis can perform MPI on accessible bridge details where the owner arranges access, traffic control and safety. The owner or engineer sets the scope and decides what to do with cracks; we report indications with location and size against the specification.

faq.q: What does an MPI report contain?
faq.a: It lists the component, procedure and revision, equipment and calibration dates, particle type, light readings for fluorescent work, technician and level, and surface condition. Each indication is recorded with location, length and orientation, and marked accepted or rejected against the code.

faq.q: How do I request a quote for MPI in Kansas City?
faq.a: Send component details, material, access conditions, the governing code and your preferred dates using the quote form. We reply within one business day with a scope and quotation.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing in Kansas City, MO | Dye PT
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection in Kansas City, MO for stainless and aluminum welds, castings and process equipment, performed at your plant. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Kansas City, Missouri
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing in Kansas City, Missouri: dye penetrant inspection of welds, castings and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-porous metals where a surface crack must be found. Technicians are mobilized to your plant or shop, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a penetrant testing quote for your Kansas City site and we reply within one business day.

Where dye penetrant inspection is used in Kansas City

Penetrant testing earns its place where magnetic methods cannot be used, and the Kansas City economy has plenty of non-magnetic metal. Food and beverage plants run stainless tanks, heat exchangers and sanitary piping. Biologics and animal-health manufacturers operate stainless process vessels and clean utility lines. Automotive and battery supply plants machine and weld aluminum components. Fabrication shops produce stainless and aluminum assemblies for a wide range of industries. Surface cracks in any of these can leak product, harbor contamination or grow under fatigue.

Typical PT work in this market:

  • Stainless steel weld seams on sanitary process piping, tanks and vessels, checked after fabrication or repair.
  • Heat exchanger tube-to-tubesheet welds and nozzle welds on stainless and nickel-alloy equipment.
  • Aluminum castings and machined housings, where porosity and cracks open to the surface need to be found before assembly.
  • Repair excavations in non-magnetic alloys, checked after grinding and after the final pass.
  • Pump and valve components, shafts and fittings in stainless and bronze at plants and water facilities.
  • Root and cap passes on small-bore stainless piping where a visual check alone is not enough.

What penetrant testing finds, and what it misses

Penetrant testing is a surface method. A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean, dry surface and drawn by capillary action into any flaw that is open to the surface. After the excess is removed, a developer pulls the trapped liquid back out and spreads it into a visible indication. Cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and porosity that break the surface show up clearly on almost any non-porous material, ferrous or not.

The limits are as important as the strengths. A flaw that does not reach the surface is invisible to the method, however large it is inside. Smeared metal from grinding, blasting or machining can close a crack mouth and hide it, which is why heavy cleaning and, where the procedure demands, etching come before penetrant is applied. Rough, porous or heavily coated surfaces hold penetrant and cause false indications. Penetrant also says nothing about wall thickness, so corrosion mapping stays with ultrasonic testing.

The process, step by step

A penetrant examination follows a fixed sequence, and each step has a minimum time or condition in the procedure. The surface is cleaned and dried, and the technician checks that no coating, scale or oil remains. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left for its dwell time, long enough for capillary action to fill fine cracks. Excess is removed according to the system used: wiped with solvent for solvent-removable systems, or rinsed with controlled water or emulsified first for water-washable and post-emulsifiable ones.

A thin, even layer of developer is then applied, and the part is examined within the time window in the procedure. Color-contrast systems are viewed in good white light; fluorescent systems are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area and are more sensitive. For field work on welds, solvent-removable visible penetrant is the most common choice because the kit is portable and needs no water supply or darkened booth. After the examination, the part is cleaned of penetrant residue.

Surface preparation and cleaning before penetrant

A penetrant result is only as honest as the cleaning behind it. On Kansas City process equipment, the contaminants differ by industry: oils and food residues in beverage plants, product film and cleaning chemicals in pharmaceutical vessels, cutting fluids and release agents on machined aluminum. Each needs a cleaner that removes it without leaving a residue that blocks the flaw. Weld spatter, slag and heat tint are removed mechanically, and the area is then cleaned with solvent and allowed to dry fully, because moisture or solvent trapped in a crack keeps penetrant out.

Mechanical treatment needs care. Wire brushing, grinding, blasting or sanding can peen the surface and smear metal over a crack mouth, particularly on soft alloys such as aluminum. Where the code allows, a light etch after mechanical cleaning reopens the surface. On sanitary stainless, the finish is also a quality requirement, so the owner should say how much surface change is acceptable. These decisions are made in the procedure before the first indication is read, not on the day.

Temperature, contamination and the materials common in Kansas City

ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard temperature range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Outside that range the procedure has to be qualified for the temperature in use. Kansas City winters put a cold plant floor or an outdoor pipe rack below the range, and a sun-heated stainless tank in summer can be above it. The practical answer is to warm the part, shade it or use a procedure qualified for the actual temperature.

Contamination control matters on the stainless and nickel alloys common in food, pharma and chemical plants. Penetrant materials used on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys are controlled for halogen and sulfur content, because residues left on these metals can promote cracking in service. The technician keeps the lot certifications for the penetrant, remover and developer, and a thorough post-clean after the examination is part of the job on sanitary equipment.

Codes and acceptance criteria

Technique is set in ASME Section V Article 6 and in ASTM E165 for general industry. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 where penetrant testing is used on structural welds. The Article 6 requirements explained page walks through the controls. In general, linear indications and rounded indications are judged against different limits, and the report states which table was applied.

Missouri's Division of Fire Safety administers the state boiler and pressure vessel law, with certificate inspections the responsibility of the owner. If API 510 or API 570 governs the equipment, the owner's authorized inspector directs the inspection and Atlantis reports the surface indications found. Food and pharmaceutical customers also carry their own quality-system requirements for weld records, and those requirements are met through the contract and the report format.

Who does the work, and what the report contains

A Level II technician qualified under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, performs and interprets the penetrant examination. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the results: Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own technicians, so a customer should ask to see the written practice.

The report names the component, the procedure and revision, the penetrant system and lot numbers, the cleaning method, the dwell and development times, the part temperature, the lighting used, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is described by type, position and size, with a sketch or photograph, and marked accepted or rejected against the named table. Repairs and re-examinations are recorded the same way.

Planning a penetrant job in Kansas City

Most of the planning comes down to temperature, cleanliness and access. In winter, plan for heat or enclosure around the test area and bring penetrant materials in from the cold. In summer, shade hot surfaces. Humid air can slow solvent flash-off, and wind blows developer unevenly, so outdoor tank and pipe-rack work needs windbreaks. Plant outages and shutdown seasons in spring and fall fill quickly.

Atlantis has no office in Kansas City, so technicians travel to your site; travel for the agreed scope is included in the quotation. At food and pharmaceutical plants, tell us about site hygiene rules, gowning and permitted chemicals before the visit, because penetrant materials may need approval. Tell us the component list, material, joint type, surface condition and code for a quotation.

Weld joints and components: what to expect

On a stainless butt weld the technician examines the cap, the toes on both sides and the heat-affected zone, looking for linear indications such as crater cracks or toe cracks and for rounded indications such as surface porosity. On a nozzle or tube-to-tubesheet weld, access determines the technique, and a small mirror or a flexible light may be needed. On castings and machined housings, the focus is on thin sections, sharp corners and fastener holes, where shrinkage porosity and cracks cluster. Each of these gets a defined view, and the report states which areas were examined.

Because penetrant indications bleed over time, the technician reads them within the development window and photographs or sketches them before they spread. A suspect indication can be wiped away and the part re-processed to see whether it returns, which separates true cracks from smears and cleaning residue. Clear results are recorded as well; a report that lists only defects makes it hard to tell what was actually covered. Retained records also let the owner's quality group audit the work later without calling the technician back.

PT, MT or UT for your Kansas City job

If the part is carbon steel and you are looking for a surface crack, magnetic particle inspection in Kansas City is often faster. If the material is non-magnetic, penetrant is the practical surface method. If you need the inside of a weld or the remaining wall, use ultrasonic testing in Kansas City. See the MT versus PT comparison and the national penetrant testing service page for the full scope.

Training your own PT technicians

Employers who want to qualify their own staff can use PT Level 1 training, PT Level 2 training and the penetrant practice simulator, with employer-led practical checks recorded under the written practice. The Kansas City training page explains the format. For a written practice or procedure, our written practice development service is available.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Kansas City for penetrant testing?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Kansas City. Technicians are mobilized to your plant or shop with the penetrant kit, lighting and a written procedure for the agreed scope, and the quotation includes travel.

faq.q: What kinds of flaws can liquid penetrant testing find?
faq.a: Only flaws open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and surface porosity. A flaw below the surface will not show, however large, so penetrant is paired with ultrasonic testing when internal quality matters.

faq.q: Which materials can be inspected with penetrant?
faq.a: Almost any non-porous material: stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium, copper alloys, carbon steel and many ceramics. Porous materials absorb penetrant and give false results. It is the main surface method for metals that magnetic particle testing cannot examine.

faq.q: What temperatures can penetrant testing be done at?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 covers 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both the part and the materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the temperature used, so cold or hot Kansas City conditions may require heating, shading or a qualified procedure.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much for dye penetrant?
faq.a: Penetrant has to get into the flaw. Paint, scale, oil, or metal smeared over a crack by grinding keep the liquid out and give a false clear result. Cleaning, and etching where the procedure calls for it, come before the penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Is there a concern about penetrant on stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. Materials used on austenitic stainless and nickel alloys are controlled for halogen and sulfur content, and residues are removed afterward. The technician keeps the lot certifications and the report records the materials used.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible penetrant is a colored dye viewed in white light and is common in the field. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light in a dark area and is more sensitive, so it is chosen for fine cracks and critical parts.

faq.q: What does a penetrant inspection report include?
faq.a: The component, procedure and revision, penetrant system and lot numbers, cleaning method, dwell and development times, part temperature, lighting, technician and level, and each indication with position, size and accept or reject against the named code.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for penetrant testing in Kansas City?
faq.a: Use the quote form to send the component list, material, surface condition, code and preferred dates. We reply within one business day with scope, procedure and quotation.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing Kansas City, MO | UT Alternatives
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. In Kansas City, MO we offer UT as a volumetric alternative, Level III image review and RT theory training.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Kansas City, Missouri
rt.html:
To be direct, Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing anywhere in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity: sources and X-ray equipment are regulated by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under 10 CFR Part 34, or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers in Kansas City or anywhere else in the country. If you searched for RT in Kansas City, this page explains what Atlantis does offer instead.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative in Kansas City

Where the construction code and the owner allow it, ultrasonic examination can take the place of radiography for weld volume. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits it in place of radiography only under specific conditions. None of these is automatic. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector before the job.

Atlantis performs ultrasonic weld and thickness examination for Kansas City owners, with technicians mobilized to your site. See ultrasonic testing in Kansas City for scope and technique, and request a UT quote if you want to discuss whether it fits your weld.

Level III review of radiographs and RT procedures

Some of the most valuable radiography work needs no radiation licence at all, because it is done on the images. An ASNT Level III can review radiographs, on film or as digital images, and the technique sheets that go with them against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical requests include a second read on a disputed indication, a check that image quality indicators and density or exposure criteria were met, and a review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice before work begins.

Atlantis's Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. These reviews are done as independent opinions for the owner; we do not name or recommend a radiography contractor. Details of the wider offer are on the Level III consulting page, and procedure and practice support is covered by written practice development.

Radiographic testing theory and training

For employers that want to build their own radiography capability, the classroom and exam-preparation part can be done separately from the licensed field work. Atlantis offers theory instruction on the method under SNT-TC-1A: see the radiographic testing Level 2 course and the Kansas City training page. Your employer certifies its own technicians, and radiation safety training and licensing remain with the licensee and the regulator.

Other Atlantis services in Kansas City

If the underlying need is surface-crack detection or wall measurement, other methods may answer it more directly: magnetic particle inspection in Kansas City for carbon steel and liquid penetrant testing in Kansas City for non-magnetic metal. Atlantis has no office in Kansas City, so technicians travel to your site for any of these services. Send the component list, material, code and access conditions through the quote form, and we will tell you plainly which method fits the question you need answered, including when the honest answer is that a licensed radiography contractor is the right choice.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Kansas City?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in this country, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules, 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State. It is not a service we offer here.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it under specific conditions. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector must agree to the substitution before the work starts.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. Our Level III reads the film or digital images and technique sheets against the Article 2 rules in ASME Section V and the construction code, gives a second opinion on disputed indications and examines the contractor's procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Does Atlantis recommend radiography contractors in Kansas City?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. If you need radiography, choose a licensed contractor of your own; we can then review the procedure or images independently for you.

faq.q: Is there a radiographic testing course I can take?
faq.a: Yes. Theory instruction for radiographic testing is available through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Your employer certifies technicians under its written practice, and radiation safety and licensing are separate and handled by the licensee.
